articles.title: A Common Diabetes Pill Erased Heart Failure in People Born With a Risky Gene. The Trial Result Is Stunning.
articles.excerpt: Re-analysing the 12,000-patient DECLARE-TIMI 58 trial, Harvard and MIT researchers found that dapagliflozin — an inexpensive SGLT2 inhibitor already used for type 2 diabetes — cut heart-failure hospitalisation about eight times more powerfully in people carrying inherited cardiomyopathy gene variants. Among carriers with no prior heart failure, none on the drug developed it, against 12.8 per cent on placebo.
articles.image_caption: A model of the human heart; an SGLT2 diabetes drug sharply cut heart-failure risk in carriers of cardiomyopathy genes
articles.nri_angle: South Asians carry both an unusually high burden of type 2 diabetes — the exact population already prescribed SGLT2 inhibitors — and a documented predisposition to inherited cardiac disease and young-onset heart failure, so a cheap drug many NRIs already swallow daily may double as a genetic-risk shield, making family history and genetic testing newly worth discussing with a doctor.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Four Minutes a Day Rebuilt Strength in 74-Year-Olds. The Routine Needs No Gym and No Hour You Do Not Have.
articles.excerpt: A Penn State trial published in PLOS One tested a stripped-down programme of four moves — push-ups, chair stands, two-arm rows and stair stepping, 30 seconds each — in adults averaging 74. Marked gains in physical function showed up in just 12 weeks, dismantling the biggest excuse older adults give for skipping strength work: that it takes too long.
articles.image_caption: An older adult exercising with a resistance band, the kind of minimal strength work the FAST-2 trial tested
articles.nri_angle: Ageing NRI parents and grandparents — often sedentary, intimidated by gyms, and culturally unaccustomed to formal strength training — are exactly the group at highest risk of the rapid muscle loss that steals independence, and a four-minute, no-equipment routine doable in a living room removes nearly every barrier the diaspora's elders cite.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: It Is Not Just How Long You Sleep — It Is When. A 7,270-Person Study Ties Late Nights to Diabetes.
articles.excerpt: Analysing a nationally representative US health survey, researchers found that night owls and people whose weekend sleep drifts more than half an hour from their weekday schedule carried a roughly 45 per cent higher odds of diabetes. The striking part: a high-quality diet substantially blunted the damage from that weekend drift — a finding with direct force for a diaspora that eats late, works across time zones, and prides itself on home cooking.
articles.image_caption: A person asleep at night; new research links late and irregular sleep timing to higher diabetes risk
articles.nri_angle: South Asian households are famous for late dinners, midnight family calls across continents and weekend schedules that swing wildly from weekday ones — the exact 'social jet lag' this study links to diabetes — yet the same research shows the diaspora's home-cooked, vegetable-and-pulse-heavy diet can be a genuine shield, making this a rare piece of actionable, culturally specific science.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Cutting Sugar to Zero Backfired. A New Study Found Sugar-Free Diets Disrupted the Gut and Triggered Fatty Liver.
articles.excerpt: Presented at the Endocrine Society's ENDO 2026 meeting, a 16-week study found that mice on a sucrose-free low-fat diet developed impaired glucose control, insulin resistance, gut microbial imbalance, intestinal inflammation and fatty liver changes — despite no difference in body weight. The lesson for a diaspora bombarded with 'quit sugar' wellness advice: the goal is balance, not elimination.
articles.image_caption: Refined sugar, which a new study suggests should be moderated rather than eliminated entirely
articles.nri_angle: The 'no sugar challenge' has swept diaspora wellness circles — WhatsApp diet groups, Indian fitness influencers, Navratri and Ekadashi-adjacent cleanses — yet this research suggests that for a population already prone to insulin resistance and lean fatty liver, swinging to total sugar elimination from a low-fat diet may do real metabolic harm rather than good.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: South Asians Are Already in Trouble by 45 — Even the Ones Eating Right. A 2,700-Person Study Found the Window.
articles.excerpt: Combining two decades-long American cohorts, Northwestern researchers found that South Asian adults arrive at midlife with the highest rates of prediabetes and high blood pressure of any group — despite reporting healthier diets, less alcohol and lower body weight. At 45, nearly a third of South Asian men already had prediabetes, against just 4 per cent of white men. The paradox points to a risk that builds long before the diet advice ever arrives.
articles.image_caption: A clinician checks a patient's blood pressure, one of the risk factors South Asians show at strikingly young ages
articles.nri_angle: The study draws on South Asian adults living in America and pinpoints the early-40s as the window when diabetes and hypertension risk is already high but still preventable — a direct, actionable message for NRI families who assume that eating well and staying slim is enough to keep heart disease at bay.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: The Carb War Has a Verdict, and It Is Not Keto. For the Rice-and-Roti Diaspora, the News Is Better Than Expected.
articles.excerpt: Two strands of new research land on the same conclusion: very-low-carb and ketogenic diets deliver sharp gains on a few markers but raise 'bad' cholesterol, while moderate-carb eating improves health across a broader range of measures — and whole grains, eaten by the serving, slow the spread of the waistline and blunt rising blood sugar. For South Asians told to fear every grain of rice, the distinction that matters is refined versus whole, not carb versus no-carb.
articles.image_caption: Whole grains such as brown rice and millet, which research links to slower waistline growth and steadier blood sugar
articles.nri_angle: South Asian diets are built on rice, wheat and pulses, and the diaspora is frequently nudged toward extreme low-carb or keto regimes that are culturally alienating — the new evidence suggests a moderate, whole-grain-forward approach is both healthier across more measures and far easier to sustain on an Indian plate.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: You Can Be Slim and Still Have a Dangerous Fatty Liver. For South Asians, the Standard Tests Often Miss It.
articles.excerpt: Up to 45 per cent of fatty liver disease in Asian populations occurs in people of normal weight, and the lean form carries an equal or higher risk of death, cirrhosis and liver cancer than the obese kind. Worse, the blood-test scores doctors rely on to flag liver scarring were built on white patients — and a body of research shows they systematically under-detect damage in South Asians.
articles.image_caption: A medical illustration of the human liver, the organ at the centre of South Asia's hidden fatty-liver epidemic
articles.nri_angle: South Asians develop fatty liver disease at normal body weights and lower BMIs than other groups, yet the non-invasive blood-score tests doctors use to screen for liver scarring were validated mainly on white patients and have been shown to miss advanced disease in South Asian patients — leaving many diaspora adults falsely reassured by a 'normal' result.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Air Pollution Is Ageing the Brain and Driving Dementia. A Half-Million-Person Study Just Mapped How.
articles.excerpt: Tracking 488,000 adults, researchers found that the most polluted air raised dementia risk by up to 20 per cent — and traced the mechanism to accelerated biological ageing and visible shrinkage of the brain. For a diaspora whose parents and relatives live in some of the world's dirtiest air, the findings move pollution from an abstract worry to a measurable threat to the mind.
articles.image_caption: Smog blankets a city skyline, the kind of fine-particle pollution now tied to faster brain ageing and dementia
articles.nri_angle: Many NRIs have aging parents and relatives living in Indian cities that rank among the most polluted on earth, and a major new study quantifying how fine-particle pollution accelerates brain aging and dementia risk turns a familiar background anxiety into concrete grounds for action — from air purifiers to relocation decisions.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Why South Asians Get Heart Disease Younger Has Never Been Answered. A New Genomic Biobank Is Built to Find Out.
articles.excerpt: The OurHealth Study, a decentralised digital biobank run by the Broad Institute, Harvard, Stanford and Yale, is sequencing the DNA of South Asian Americans from their kitchen tables — and handing them back personalised heart-risk scores. It is one of the first serious attempts to close a genomic blind spot that has left the diaspora flying blind.
articles.image_caption: DNA sequencing in a genomics laboratory, the technology behind the OurHealth biobank
articles.nri_angle: South Asians carry more than double the cardiometabolic disease risk of other groups yet are almost absent from the genomic datasets that drive modern risk prediction and drug development — a gap the OurHealth biobank is specifically designed to close for the US diaspora.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Vitamin D Cuts Diabetes Risk — but Only If Your Genes Cooperate. A New Study Explains Who Actually Benefits.
articles.excerpt: Tufts researchers analysing DNA from over 2,000 trial participants found that vitamin D meaningfully lowered the risk of type 2 diabetes in people with certain variations of the vitamin D receptor gene, and did nothing for the roughly one in three who carry a different variant. For a diaspora plagued by both vitamin D deficiency and diabetes, it is a clue worth understanding.
articles.image_caption: Vitamin D supplement capsules, whose diabetes-prevention benefit may depend on a person's genes
articles.nri_angle: South Asians suffer from unusually high rates of both vitamin D deficiency and type 2 diabetes, making the question of who actually benefits from supplementation — and why the answer may be written in their genes — directly relevant to millions of diaspora families.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: The Nightly Drink Was Never Harmless. A Review of 7,200 Studies Just Put a Number on the Risk.
articles.excerpt: Research published in the Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs finds the safest amount of alcohol is none — and that the old ‘two drinks a day’ limit carries a 1-in-25 lifetime risk of death. For a diaspora where social drinking is rising fastest among the young and the affluent, the math is worth reading carefully.
articles.image_caption: Giles Watson's poetry and prose via flickr (BY-SA)
articles.nri_angle: Alcohol consumption is climbing fastest among young, affluent, and urban Indians and second-generation diaspora professionals, even as the community already carries elevated liver-disease and cancer susceptibility — making a clear-eyed read of the new dose-risk math especially relevant to NRI families.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A Decade of Brain Scans Shows the MIND Diet Slows Ageing in the Brain. The Indian Plate Is Halfway There.
articles.excerpt: A Framingham Heart Study analysis published in the Journal of Neurology, Neurosurgery & Psychiatry tracked brain structure over ten years and found that people who stuck closest to the MIND diet had measurably younger-looking brains. Much of what it rewards — leafy greens, beans, whole grains — already lives in the diaspora kitchen.
articles.image_caption: Leafy greens, the dietary foundation the MIND diet links to slower brain ageing
articles.nri_angle: The MIND diet's brain-protective core — leafy greens, legumes, whole grains, and nuts — overlaps heavily with traditional Indian regional cooking, giving diaspora families a built-in advantage against cognitive decline if they resist the drift toward fried and ultraprocessed convenience food.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Just 90 Minutes of Lifting a Week Cuts Death Risk. For South Asians, There Is No Cheaper Insurance Policy.
articles.excerpt: A 147,000-person study spanning three decades, published in the British Journal of Sports Medicine, found the clearest survival benefit at 90 to 119 minutes of weekly resistance training — a finding that matters acutely for a community that loses muscle faster and earlier than almost any other.
articles.image_caption: Resistance training delivers outsized survival benefits, new research finds (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: South Asians carry less skeletal muscle and more visceral fat at any given weight, so the protective payoff from a modest weekly lifting habit is disproportionately large for the diaspora's aging parents and midlife professionals.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Working From Home Made You an Hour Lonelier Every Day. A Half-Million-Person Study Just Proved It.
articles.excerpt: Remote workers in 'remotable' jobs — overwhelmingly in tech — spend an extra hour alone each workday and don't make up for it after hours. For South Asian professionals 10,000 miles from family, the numbers hit differently.
articles.image_caption: A man working alone from home on his laptop in a quiet indoor setting
articles.nri_angle: Indian-origin tech professionals are disproportionately in 'remotable' jobs, and they already carry the baseline isolation of living thousands of miles from extended family — making the mental health costs of remote work a doubled burden.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: South Asian Women Hit Menopause Four Years Before the American Average. The Wellness Industry Has Barely Noticed.
articles.excerpt: A major study of South Asian American women finds the mean age at natural menopause is 48 — four years earlier than the US norm of 52. Nearly a third experienced premature or early menopause. Apple just launched a programme for everyone else.
articles.image_caption: A middle-aged woman working out on a gym machine for a healthy lifestyle
articles.nri_angle: South Asian American women enter menopause years earlier than the national average, face more severe symptoms, and navigate cultural taboos that discourage open discussion — a triple burden the mainstream wellness industry has yet to address.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Your Grandmother's Filter Kaapi May Be the Best Diabetes Drug Nobody Prescribed. A Genetic Study Just Showed How.
articles.excerpt: Unsweetened filter coffee uniquely promotes a gut bacterium that lowers blood sugar — and the mechanism maps perfectly onto the South Indian decoction ritual millions of diaspora families still follow.
articles.image_caption: A tumbler and davara of South Indian filter coffee, the traditional serving style found in homes and cafes across Tamil Nadu and Karnataka
articles.nri_angle: Millions of NRI families from South India still use the stainless-steel filter their parents brought over — and new genetic evidence suggests this exact brewing method has unique diabetes-prevention properties relevant to a community with elevated Type 2 risk.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Yoga Mats at the Lincoln Memorial, a Guru at Times Square. The Diaspora's Yoga Day Has Grown Up.
articles.excerpt: The 11th International Day of Yoga arrives themed around healthy ageing — and for NRIs managing parents' health across oceans, the timing could not be sharper.
articles.image_caption: Yoga practitioners at an International Day of Yoga celebration
articles.nri_angle: International Day of Yoga events across US cities offer NRIs practical tools for managing their own and their parents' healthy ageing from abroad.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Ozempic Users Are Exercising Less, Not More. For South Asians, That Is a Dangerous Trade-Off.
articles.excerpt: A study of 753 GLP-1 users found daily steps fell 11 per cent and active minutes dropped 21 per cent after starting treatment. Muscle loss is the hidden cost.
articles.image_caption: A GLP-1 receptor agonist medication pen
articles.nri_angle: South Asians are among the fastest-growing users of GLP-1 drugs but face compounding muscle-loss risk due to lower baseline skeletal muscle mass.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Your Gut Bacteria Decide How Many Calories You Actually Absorb. A New Model Just Proved It.
articles.excerpt: Arizona State researchers built a mathematical model that tracks food beyond the label. For South Asians losing their traditional diet, the implications are enormous.
articles.image_caption: Illustration of human gut microbiota — new research shows these bacteria determine how many calories the body actually absorbs (Wikimedia Commons)

sources.label: PLOS ONE - Davis et al., Modeling the microbial contribution to human energy balance using the DAMM model, May 2026
npj Biofilms and Microbiomes - The adoption of a westernized gut microbiome in Indian Immigrants and Indo-Canadians

articles.nri_angle: Indian immigrants lose beneficial gut bacteria like Prevotella copri when they abandon traditional dal-and-roti diets, potentially absorbing over 100 extra hidden calories daily on Western food.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A Heat Wave Is Sweeping the US as the World Cup Kicks Off. South Asians Are Uniquely at Risk.
articles.excerpt: More than 200,000 heat deaths in Europe since 2022. A scorching American summer ahead. And a diaspora population that thinks it knows heat but is dangerously wrong about this kind.
articles.image_caption: Mr.TinDC via flickr (BY-ND)

sources.label: World Health Organization - Heat deaths in Europe report, June 2026
CNN Health - US heat wave health guidance, June 2026

articles.nri_angle: NRIs attending World Cup games and hosting elderly parents from India this summer face unique heat risks that Indian heat tolerance does not prepare them for.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A $2 Tuberculosis Vaccine Just Normalised Blood Sugar in Type 1 Diabetics. South Asians Should Pay Attention.
articles.excerpt: BCG shots reprogrammed malfunctioning white blood cells and slashed insulin use in adults with lifelong Type 1 diabetes — bypassing the pancreas entirely.
articles.image_caption: An adult with Type 1 diabetes wearing an insulin pump and continuous glucose monitor
articles.nri_angle: South Asians have the second-highest Type 1 diabetes incidence globally, and BCG is already manufactured at scale by India's Serum Institute — making this both a medical and supply-chain story for the diaspora.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Losing Belly Fat Saved Brains for a Decade. Losing Weight Did Not. Why South Asians Cannot Ignore This Study.
articles.excerpt: A 16-year MRI study of 533 adults found that visceral fat — not body weight — drives brain shrinkage. South Asians carry more of it than almost any other group.
articles.image_caption: MRI brain imaging used to track long-term effects of visceral fat on cognitive function
articles.nri_angle: South Asians carry disproportionately high visceral fat at normal BMI — this study shows that invisible belly fat, not weight, drives brain ageing and dementia risk, making it directly relevant to diaspora health screening.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Five Fruits a Day May Not Save Your Heart. A 30,000-Person Study Says It Is the Type That Matters.
articles.excerpt: Fewer than one in four adults hit the flavanol threshold linked to cardiovascular protection — but traditional South Asian staples like green tea, fava beans and berries could close the gap overnight.
articles.image_caption: Berries rich in flavanols — a new study of 30,000 people finds specific fruit compounds, not total servings, protect heart health
articles.nri_angle: South Asian diets already rich in green tea, fava beans and berries may give the diaspora a natural advantage in meeting the flavanol threshold that Western diets consistently miss.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: High Social Media Use Raises Mental Health Risks in Teens. A Landmark Australian Study Just Quantified the Damage.
articles.excerpt: A population-based cohort of 13-to-16-year-olds shows heavy social media use is linked to depression, anxiety and cyberbullying — and a separate trial found that just cutting back reduces loneliness within weeks.
articles.image_caption: A landmark Australian study links heavy social media use to rising anxiety and depression among teenagers
articles.nri_angle: Diaspora parents navigating screen time rules across two cultural contexts now have hard data: heavy social media use in teens is causally linked to loneliness, and modest reductions produce measurable mental health gains.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: America's Doctors Are About to Learn About Food for the First Time. Here Is Why NRI Patients Should Care.
articles.excerpt: Seventy-three medical schools have pledged 40 hours of nutrition training. Licensing exams will test it. For South Asian patients whose food traditions were routinely dismissed, this is a watershed.
articles.image_caption: A nutritionist discusses healthy eating with a client surrounded by fresh produce
articles.nri_angle: South Asian patients have long faced physicians untrained in nutrition who dismissed food-based wellness traditions; this overhaul could finally bridge that gap.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Your Frozen Paratha May Be Wrecking Your Gut. A 124,000-Person Study Just Singled Out Ultraprocessed Grains.
articles.excerpt: The largest global study of its kind found that ultraprocessed grain intake nearly doubled the risk of inflammatory bowel disease. Fresh bread and rice were protective. The implications for diaspora kitchens are enormous.
articles.image_caption: Close-up of sliced whole grain bread on a wooden surface with wheat ears
articles.nri_angle: The shift from fresh roti and home-ground flour to frozen parathas, packaged naan, and instant noodles in NRI kitchens mirrors exactly the dietary transition this study links to gut disease.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Your Brain Starts Changing After Two Minutes of Meditation. Indian Scientists Just Proved It.
articles.excerpt: NIMHANS Bengaluru and Harvard tracked 103 meditators second-by-second and found the seven-minute sweet spot for breath-watching meditation.
articles.image_caption: A practitioner in focused breath-watching meditation
articles.nri_angle: An ancient Indian meditation practice studied at India's NIMHANS by Indian-origin Harvard researchers — validating what diaspora families practised for generations.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: The $275 Million Turmeric Myth: Why South Asian Kitchens Got It Right and the Supplement Industry Got It Wrong
articles.excerpt: Thirty papers retracted, curcumin barely detectable in the bloodstream, and turmeric supplements are now the top cause of herbal liver injury in the US. Here is what the diaspora needs to know.
articles.image_caption: Turmeric root and powder — safe in cooking, but concentrated supplements carry liver risks
articles.nri_angle: South Asian families have used turmeric in cooking for millennia — the supplement industry concentrated it into dangerous doses, while the kitchen had the right amount all along.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Scientists Just Mapped the 'Zombie Cells' Driving Ageing. The Implications for Your Parents Are Enormous.
articles.excerpt: A landmark NIH consortium has built the first comprehensive atlas of senescent cells across the human body, identifying blood biomarkers that predict kidney disease, frailty, and diabetes — and opening the door to drugs that could selectively destroy them.
articles.image_caption: Microscopy image of senescent cells — the 'zombie cells' that accumulate with ageing and drive chronic disease (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: With ageing parents back in India or living with family abroad, senolytic therapies could transform how the diaspora manages eldercare across borders.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: High Blood Pressure May Actually Protect Frail Elders From Dementia. A 6,000-Person Study Just Upended the Textbook.
articles.excerpt: A nine-year Neurology study found that elevated blood pressure cut dementia risk by 32 per cent in frail older adults — while raising it by 39 per cent in robust ones. For families managing ageing parents across borders, the implications are urgent.
articles.image_caption: Blood pressure measurement — a new study challenges conventional wisdom about hypertension management in frail elderly patients (Wikimedia Commons)

sources.label: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill

articles.nri_angle: NRIs coordinating eldercare remotely need to understand that blood pressure targets for frail parents may differ sharply from standard guidelines — a conversation to have with doctors in India.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Three Common Sleep Habits Are Silently Ageing Your Brain. A 23,000-Person Study Just Identified Them.
articles.excerpt: Sleeping too little, napping too often, and struggling to fall asleep were each independently linked to white matter damage — a marker of dementia risk.
articles.image_caption: An MRI brain scan showing white matter hyperintensities linked to cognitive decline
articles.nri_angle: South Asian communities face compounding sleep disruptors — intergenerational households, long-haul India travel, and cultural normalisation of napping — that make these findings especially urgent.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: South Asians Do Everything Right for Heart Health and Still Get Sick Earlier. A 2,700-Person Study Finally Explains Why.
articles.excerpt: Northwestern researchers found elevated rates of prediabetes, diabetes, and hypertension in South Asian Americans by age 45 — despite healthier diets and lower alcohol use.
articles.image_caption: A blood pressure check — South Asian Americans show elevated cardiovascular risk factors by age 45 despite healthier habits
articles.nri_angle: South Asian Americans face a paradox: healthier habits yet higher cardiovascular risk by midlife, demanding earlier screening and South Asian-specific BMI thresholds.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Four Minutes of Exercise a Day Quadrupled Fitness in Adults Over 65. For the Diaspora, This Changes Everything About Aging Parents.
articles.excerpt: A Penn State study found that push-ups, chair stands, rows and stair steps — just 30 seconds each — produced dramatic strength gains in 12 weeks. The implications for NRI families managing elder care across oceans are profound.
articles.image_caption: A senior man performing push-ups at home as part of a daily fitness routine
articles.nri_angle: For millions of NRI families managing aging parents' health from thousands of miles away, a research-backed four-minute daily routine that requires no gym and no equipment beyond resistance bands could be the most practical intervention they can actually implement remotely.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Men and Women Need Different Diets to Live Longer. A 104,000-Person Study Just Proved It.
articles.excerpt: Coffee extends male lifespan by up to three years. Fish does the same for women. Both sexes benefit from cutting processed food — but the optimal longevity diet is not one-size-fits-all, and the South Asian kitchen may already hold the advantage.
articles.image_caption: Grilled fish with fresh vegetables and spices — the Mediterranean staples linked to female longevity
articles.nri_angle: The study's findings align strikingly well with traditional Indian dietary patterns — high legume and vegetable intake, extensive use of spices and turmeric, fish-heavy coastal cuisines, and daily coffee or tea rituals — suggesting that diaspora families preserving these food traditions may already be on the right track.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk
